content: Mometasone furoate is a corticosteroid approved by the FDA for treating inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses in patients aged 2 years and older. Common adverse reactions include burning, itching, and skin atrophy. The cream is applied as a thin film to affected areas once daily and is for external use only. It is not recommended for use in children under 2 years of age, and its safety and efficacy for use beyond three weeks in pediatric patients have not been established. Therapy should be discontinued once control is achieved, and if no improvement is observed within two weeks, the diagnosis should be reassessed. Mometasone furoate cream should not be used with occlusive dressings unless directed by a physician and should not be applied to the diaper area in children who require diapers or plastic pants, as these garments may act as occlusive dressings. The cream is not intended for oral, ophthalmic, or intravaginal use and should be avoided on the face, groin, or axillae unless directed by a physician. Systemic absorption of topical corticosteroids can lead to reversible hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression and potential glucocorticoid insufficiency. This may occur during treatment or after withdrawal. Manifestations of Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and glucosuria can also result from systemic absorption. Factors predisposing patients to HPA axis suppression include the use of high-potency steroids, large treatment surface areas, prolonged use, occlusive dressings, altered skin barrier, liver failure, and young age. Periodic evaluation for HPA axis suppression may be necessary, which can be assessed using the ACTH stimulation test. In a study involving adult subjects with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis, the application of 15 grams of mometasone furoate cream twice daily for seven days caused a slight reduction in adrenal corticosteroid secretion. If HPA axis suppression is noted, the drug should be gradually withdrawn, application frequency reduced, or substituted with a less potent corticosteroid. Recovery of HPA axis function is generally prompt upon discontinuation, but signs of glucocorticoid insufficiency may require supplemental systemic corticosteroids. Pediatric patients are more susceptible to systemic toxicity due to their larger skin surface-to-body mass ratios. They are at greater risk of HPA axis suppression, Cushing’s syndrome, and adrenal insufficiency during or after treatment withdrawal. Pediatric patients may also be more prone to skin atrophy, including striae, when treated with topical corticosteroids. Mometasone furoate cream should not be used to treat diaper dermatitis. Adverse reactions reported in clinical trials include burning, itching, skin atrophy, stinging, and furunculosis. Rarely, allergic contact dermatitis may occur, diagnosed by failure to heal rather than clinical exacerbation. If irritation develops, the cream should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. Concomitant skin infections should be treated with appropriate antifungal or antibacterial agents, and the cream should be discontinued if a favorable response is not achieved promptly. Mometasone furoate cream is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. It should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Corticosteroids have been shown to be teratogenic in laboratory animals when administered systemically at low doses. Mometasone furoate caused fetal malformations, reduced fetal growth, and dystocia in animal studies. It is unknown whether topical administration results in sufficient systemic absorption to produce detectable quantities in human milk. Caution is advised when administering the cream to nursing women. Clinical studies in geriatric patients did not identify differences in safety or effectiveness compared to younger patients, but greater sensitivity in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of mometasone furoate in relation to gender, race, renal impairment, hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. The pharmacological action of mometasone furoate involves anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive properties. Its mechanism of action is thought to involve the induction of phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins, collectively called lipocortins, which inhibit the release of arachidonic acid, a precursor of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes. The cream is supplied in 15-gram and 45-gram tubes and should be stored at controlled room temperature (20°-25°C or 68°-77°F). Patients should use the cream as directed by their physician, avoid contact with the eyes, and not use it on the face, underarms, or groin unless instructed. Treated areas should not be occluded unless directed by a physician. Therapy should be discontinued when control is achieved, and patients should report any signs of local adverse reactions to their physician.
